body.en: Statistical questions on the EST I focus on measures of centre and spread, interpreting data displays, and calculating basic probability.

Counting and probability

The probability of event \( A \) AND event \( B \) (independent): \( P(A\cap B)=P(A)\cdot P(B) \). The probability of \( A \) OR \( B \): \( P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \).

Mean \(=\dfrac{\sum x}{n}\); Median = middle value when ordered; Mode = most frequent. Range \(= \max - \min\). IQR \(= Q_3 - Q_1\). Probability: \(P(A) = \dfrac{\text{favourable}}{\text{total}}\); \(P(A \cup B) = P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B)\). Mutually exclusive: \(P(A \cap B)=0\).

A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls. Two are drawn without replacement. Find \(P(\text{both red})\).

\(P = \dfrac{4}{10} \times \dfrac{3}{9} = \dfrac{12}{90} = \dfrac{2}{15}\).

label.en: ▲ EST I Math Traps & Pitfalls — Statistics & Data Displays

body.en:
• Outlier Influence on Mean vs. Median: The mean is heavily sensitive to extreme high or low values (skewed data), whereas the median is resistant. If an extreme outlier is introduced to a data set, the mean shifts significantly toward the outlier while the median changes minimally.
  • Standard Deviation Transformations: Adding or subtracting a constant \(k\) to every data point shifts the mean by \(k\), but leaves standard deviation and IQR completely unchanged! Multiplying every value by \(c\) multiplies standard deviation by \(|c|\).
  • Two-Way Table Conditional Probability: Watch the wording of the condition! "Given that a student is female, find the probability she passed" uses the female total as the denominator. In contrast, "Find the probability that a student is female AND passed" uses the entire grand total as the denominator.
  • With vs. Without Replacement: Drawing items without replacement reduces both the numerator and the denominator on subsequent draws: \(P(\text{both red}) = \frac{R}{N} \times \frac{R-1}{N-1}\).

question.en: The ages of 7 students are: 14, 15, 15, 16, 16, 16, 18. A student is chosen at random. Find (a) the median age, (b) \(P(\text{age} > 15)\).

solution.en: (a) 4th value = 16. (b) Ages > 15: three 16s and one 18 = 4 students. \(P = 4/7\).

question.en: A survey of 200 high school students asked whether they play a varsity sport. Of 90 seniors, 36 play a varsity sport. Of 110 juniors, 55 play a varsity sport. (a) What is the probability that a randomly chosen student plays a varsity sport? (b) Given that a student is a senior, what is the probability that the student does NOT play a varsity sport?

solution.en:
(a) Probability of playing a sport: Total athletes \(= 36 + 55 = 91\). \[ P(\text{Sport}) = \dfrac{91}{200} = 0.455\, (45.5\%). \]

(b) Conditional probability for seniors: Condition on the 90 seniors (restricted denominator). The number of non-athlete seniors is \(90 - 36 = 54\): \[ P(\text{No Sport} \mid \text{Senior}) = \dfrac{54}{90} = \dfrac{3}{5} = 0.60\, (60\%). \]
